name: Zhang Yin
notes: RE-CODED excluded -> rank1 under the trade bucket's volume-ranking rule. ACN's own site claims only that it has been 'recognized as a top American exporter to China since 2001' with no ranking body named; that self-description is NOT what this anchor rests on. rev10 remains undatable for both ACN and Nine Dragons (no revenue published before the 2006 HKEX listing, whose turnover table starts at 2003), which is why rank1 applies. a2/a3 stay unknown: sources say she trained in accounting at a trade school and worked as a bookkeeper, then at a Shenzhen paper trading firm, but give no years, after two attempts in the second pilot.

name: Stephanie Shirley
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED: BusinessCloud's obituary (11 Aug 2025) states 'Her generosity would see Dame Stephanie drop out of the Sunday Times Rich List', which places her on it before the giving; several accounts call her the first person to leave the list through philanthropy. https://businesscloud.co.uk/news/tech-pioneer-dame-stephanie-steve-shirley-dies-aged-91/ BOUNDED rev10, both ends sourced. Lower end: heise online's obituary prints the early turnover series - 1964 GBP7,000, 1970 GBP50,000, 1976 GBP739,000, 'crossed the million-pound threshold' in 1977, GBP10m in 1987. GBP739,000 at the 1976 average spot rate of about 1.80 USD/GBP is roughly US$1.33M, below the 1976 nominal bar of $1,767,394. Upper end: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F_International, sourced to the Harvard Business School case (Franklin, 1986) and Let IT Go, states that by the end of the 1970s revenue had risen to GBP2.5m; at the 1979 average of about 2.12 USD/GBP that is about US$5.3M, well above the 1979 bar of $2,255,058. The conclusion is insensitive to the exact rate: the 1976 figure needs 2.39 USD/GBP to clear its bar and the 1979 figure clears its own even at parity. NOT PINNED TO 1977 on purpose: the constant-dollar bar in sterling is about GBP1.08m in 1977, GBP1.06m in 1978 and GBP1.06m in 1979, so heise's 'crossed the million-pound threshold in 1977' straddles the bar - GBP1.0m is below it, GBP1.2m above it - and the source gives no figure. The crossing is therefore bounded 1976-1979 rather than dated 1977. No IPO/acq fallback was available anyway: the March 1996 LSE float is 17-20 years late and the frame bars it here. a2: Wikipedia's honours-and-legacy section gives BSc 1956; no other source dates the degree, and 'six years of evening classes' from 1951 would suggest 1957, so conf is medium. a3: Archives of IT's timeline, 'began her IT career at the Post Office in London in 1951 at the age of 18'. a4: 1962 Freelance Programmers, per the F International article; the Steve Shirley article's phrasing around her 1959 marriage has led some obituaries to print 1959 for the founding, which is wrong. a6: March 1996 flotation on the London Stock Exchange.

name: Judy Faulkner
notes: a2 RESOLVED 1967: Wisconsin Alumni Association Distinguished Alumni profile states she "earned her BS in mathematics from Dickinson College in 1965 and her MS in Computer Sciences from UW–Madison in 1967"; incomplete doctorate is disregarded per dropout/last-completed-credential rule. https://www.uwalumni.com/news/judith-faulkner/ LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED: her Forbes profile carries a self-made score of 8, inside the roster's 6-10 band, and contemporaneous news reports of the Forbes 400 name her - she entered the 2012 Forbes 400 at No. 285 with $1.7B and ranked No. 154 in 2024. https://www.forbes.com/profile/judy-faulkner/ BOUNDED rev10, both ends sourced, and NO FALLBACK EXISTS: Epic has never listed and has never been acquired, so ipo/acq50 are unavailable and a bounded rev10 is the only legal anchor. Lower end: Acquired's Epic briefing states the company reached '$1.5 million in revenue by 1988', below the 1988 nominal bar of $3,674,564 (41% of it). Upper end: the International Directory of Company Histories entry states 'In 1997, Epic earned net income of $6.6 million on sales of $30.9 million', 6.2x the 1997 bar of $4,985,355. https://www.referenceforbusiness.com/history2/65/Epic-Systems-Corporation.html Span 1988-1997 is nine years, inside the ten-year limit. NARROWER READING NOT USED: a figure of '$18 million in 1995, up from $1.5 million in 1988' is widely repeated and would tighten the bound to 1988-1995, but two fetch attempts (acquired.fm episode page, company-histories.com / jrank mirrors of the same directory entry) failed to surface it on a page I could read, so it is not relied on. Employee counts from the same directory entry are consistent with a crossing in the early 1990s - 30 staff in 1990, 49 in 1993, 125 in 1995 against $155K of revenue per head in 1997 - but headcount times an assumed revenue-per-head is an inference, not a source, so it did not narrow the bound. a2: UNKNOWN after several attempts. Sources conflict and none pins the year: the UW-Madison CS department page lists the M.S. with no year, Forbes says she started a doctorate in 1965 and 'graduated without completing a dissertation' in the early 1970s, and The Capital Times says she founded Epic in 1979 'shortly after receiving her master's degree'. a3: JUDGMENT CALL - Forbes dates her first healthcare-computing work to 1969, the punch-card on-call scheduling system built for Dr John Greist, which is a graduate project rather than paid employment; her first clearly paid domain role, with a University of Wisconsin physicians group, is dated only to 'the early 1970s'. Confidence low. a6: Forbes named her a billionaire in March 2012, the same year she entered the Forbes 400.

name: Dietmar Hopp
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED: Forbes' billionaires profile ranks him #634 in the world with $6.4B and lists 'Source of Wealth: Software, Self Made'; German Wikipedia records rank #147 on the 2018 Forbes World's Billionaires list. https://www.forbes.com/profile/dietmar-hopp/ BOUNDED rev10, both ends sourced, IPO FALLBACK BARRED (SAP's 1988 flotation is six to twelve years after the crossing and the earlier crossing is documented). Lower end: SAP's own corporate history page for 1972-1980 states for 1976 'SAP now employs 25 people and generates DM3.81 million in revenue'. At the 1976 annual average of 2.5182 DM/US$ that is US$1.513M, below the 1976 nominal bar of $1,767,394 (86% of it). The margin is not large, but the D-Mark traded in a 2.36-2.62 band through 1976 and the figure would need a rate at or below 2.156 DM/US$ to clear the bar, so the classification holds across the whole year's range. Upper end: Computerwoche's SAP history, 'Zum zehnten Geburtstag 1982 zaehlt SAP bereits ueber 250 Firmenkunden und erzielt einen Umsatz von rund 24 Millionen Mark'; at the 1982 average of 2.4266 DM/US$ that is US$9.89M, 3.3x the 1982 bar of $2,997,425. Span 1976-1982 is six years. NOT NARROWED: SAP's own page says the company had about 60 employees by 1978 and was 'one of Germany's largest software firms', which is a qualitative claim of scale with no figure attached - under the frame that is enough to bar the IPO fallback but not enough to pin a year, and scaling 1976 revenue-per-head onto the 1978 headcount would be an inference, not a source. CONFLICTING SOURCE REJECTED: was-war-wann.de dates the same DM3.8m / small-headcount snapshot to 1980, which contradicts SAP's own 1976 dating, the 1977 Walldorf move, and its own DM24m-with-100-staff figure for 1982; SAP's page and Computerwoche agree on 1976 and were preferred. a2: German Wikipedia, Diplom-Ingenieur in Nachrichtentechnik from TH Karlsruhe in 1966. a3: BOUNDED. No source gives the year he joined IBM. English Wikipedia says 'After graduating from university, he worked as a software developer and consultant at IBM' (so not before the 1966 degree) and German Wikipedia dates his IBM Mannheim systems-consultant post to 1968-1972, so the start is bracketed to 1966-1968 rather than assumed to be 1966. a6: 1988, the year SAP became an AG and listed; Computerwoche gives DM340m of revenue in that first stock-market year.

name: Kazuhiko Nishi
notes: ROSTER UNVERIFIED, EXCLUDED BY RULE: no source list in frame.md could be confirmed to contain this person. Checked beyond the roster's claim: Women in Technology International Hall of Fame (annual 1996-2021) and Computer History Museum Fellows (annual since 1987) contain neither p14 nor p15. The frame's rule is that no name enters by free recall, so the row is excluded from every statistic rather than deleted -- the anchors below are fully researched and stand ready if a list is ever confirmed. Search was stopped deliberately at two additional lists: filtering candidate lists by whether they contain a name already chosen is post-hoc justification, not sampling. || LIST MEMBERSHIP UNCONFIRMED. Two searches (Japanese, for 長者番付 / 高額納税者番付 / 日経 and 東洋経済 rankings naming him, and for any Nikkei or Toyo Keizai ranking listing him or ASCII) produced no ranking that names Nishi. Toyo Keizai Online has published a feature ARTICLE about him ('早大1浪2留中退'名家の母を嘆かせた彼の後悔, toyokeizai.net/articles/-/743951) and Nikkei Business has interviewed him, but a bylined article is not a ranking and the roster's claim is not verified. Flagging for the reviewer rather than dropping the row. PINNED rev10, not bounded. Yamazaki Yasuo's Hosei University RIIM working paper No.24 ('パソコン黎明期のベンチャー・ビジネス - 椎名堯慶と西和彦', Japanese business-history series No.41) prints ASCII's audited fiscal-year revenue series in 表2 (units 百万円, compiled by the author from 日経新聞社編『会社総鑑』): 1977 40, 1978 142, 1979 353, 1980 835, 1981 1,634, 1982 4,200, 1983 5,047, 1984 7,756, 1985 13,884. Both sides of the crossing come from that one table. FY1979 revenue of 353 million yen at the 1979 annual average of 219.14 yen/US$ is US$1.61M, below the 1979 nominal bar of $2,255,058 (71% of it). FY1980 revenue of 835 million yen at the 1980 average of 226.74 yen/US$ is US$3.68M, above the 1980 bar of $2,559,459 (144% of it). The call is robust to the rate: 1979 would need a rate of 156.5 yen/US$ to clear its bar and 1980 would need 326 yen/US$ to fall below its own, and the yen traded roughly 194-251 in 1979 and 203-264 in 1980. The 1989 flotation is nine years late and barred. CAVEAT: en.wikipedia's ASCII article says 'In 1980, ASCII made 1.2 billion yen of sales from licensing Microsoft BASIC', which exceeds the whole-company 835 million yen in the table - most likely a calendar-year or ASCII-Microsoft-inclusive figure, since ASCII Microsoft KK was a separate 1978 entity not merged into ASCII until 1984. Either reading puts 1980 above the bar; the risk it carries is that a consolidated 1979 figure might also have cleared, which is why confidence is medium rather than high. a2: 1974, his graduation from Koyo Gakuin High School, which is the last credential he COMPLETED before his career - the same convention used for p09 Daniel Ek. He entered Waseda's mechanical engineering department in 1975 and never graduated: the working paper's chronology dates his mid-course withdrawal to 1983, three years after the crossing, and ja.wikipedia records the withdrawal with no year (Toyo Keizai calls him '1浪2留中退'). Recording that 1983 withdrawal as a2 would put education_end after first_hit, which is factually what happened but is not what this anchor measures. A doctorate from Kogakuin University followed in 1999, twenty years into his career, and is likewise not used. a4: 1976, the launch of the monthly I/O in November of that year, which the paper treats as the venture he and the later ASCII founders ran before splitting off; Nishi's own CV at nishi.org independently dates his first company, Pax Electronica, to 1976. ASCII Publishing itself was founded in May 1977 and is the hit entity. a3: no domain employment ever preceded his own ventures, so a3 is set equal to a4 at low confidence under the p01 rule; the paper describes him writing articles for the magazine コンピュートピア as an undergraduate, which would be earlier but is given no year.

name: Shola Akinlade
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED (with one caveat). YC's own company page confirms Paystack as a Y Combinator W2016 alum with status 'Acquired' (https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/paystack), and YC's published Top Companies criterion admits exits valued above $150M, which the $200M+ Stripe deal clears; search indexing of ycombinator.com/topcompanies/valuation/exits places Paystack at position 33. The Top Companies page itself renders client-side and could not be fetched directly, so the listing is corroborated rather than read off the page. FALLBACK USED, AND THE BAR ON IT WAS CHECKED. Stripe acquired Paystack in October 2020 for a reported $200M+ (TechCrunch, Reuters), far above the 2020 acq50 bar of $40,195,159. The frame bars the fallback whenever an earlier rev10 crossing is known; two attempts found no revenue figure for Paystack in any year, and the volume record argues against an earlier crossing rather than for one. Paystack's own blog milestone puts monthly transaction VALUE at 10 billion naira around September 2018 (about US$27.5M at the ~360 naira/US$ rate of that year); at Paystack's published local-card pricing of 1.5% plus 100 naira capped at 2,000 naira, that volume annualises to roughly US$4-5M of gross revenue, below the 2018 bar of $7,799,735. That arithmetic is an estimate and is used only to test whether the fallback is barred - it dates nothing. Nairametrics (Sept 2018) puts Paystack at 17,000 businesses and 'over 15% of all online payments in Nigeria', which is a real business but not the 'already industry-leading' claim that would bar the fallback; the 'more than half of all online transactions in Nigeria' and 60,000-merchant descriptions are stated as of the October 2020 acquisition itself. If Paystack's 2020 revenue did clear the $8,039,032 bar for that year, the anchor year would be 2020 under rev10 as well, so the fallback is not moving the date - the same structure as p07 Instagram. a1: no source of record gives his birth date - Wikipedia's infobox leaves it blank - so the row rests on Nigerian biography coverage (legit.ng) giving 3 March 1985; conf low. a2: BSc computer science, Babcock University, 2006 (Wikipedia, citing Nairametrics). a3: Heineken management trainee in database management, 2007-2009 per Nairametrics; he is also described as later working as a software engineer at several banks, with no years given anywhere. a4: Klein Devort, the software development and consulting company through which Precurio was built - legit.ng dates it to 2009 while other biography pages say 2008, and neither Wikipedia nor Nairametrics mentions the company at all, hence low confidence. Paystack (2015) is the hit entity, not the first venture. a6: UNKNOWN after two attempts - no scale marker after the 2020 acquisition is datable to Akinlade's own venture; the 2022 Officer of the Order of the Niger honour and the Sporting Lagos football club are recognition and a new venture, not a scale hit for Paystack.

name: Shigenobu Nagamori
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED: Nikkei's own site prints the ranking. His Nikkei Global Management Forum speaker profile (nikkeiforum.com/ngmf2016jp/speakers09.html) records that he ranked first in Nikkei Business's 2014 survey ranking of best CEOs chosen by company presidents; the Nikkei Business issue of 17 Nov 2014 is the source of the ranking, reported contemporaneously at https://www.excite.co.jp/news/article/Bizjournal_mixi201411_post-2088/ . That is a Nikkei-published ranking, not a feature article, so the roster's 'Nikkei / Toyo Keizai rankings (Japan)' citation holds. BOUNDED rev10, both ends sourced, IPO FALLBACK BARRED (the Nov 1988 Osaka/Kyoto listing is at least nine years after the crossing and Nidec's own history documents the earlier crossing). Upper end: Nidec's official 50-year history, chapter 2, dates the milestone to the fiscal year ended March 1979 - (第6期) 売上高10億円を達成, i.e. 1 billion yen of revenue in the sixth fiscal year. At the 1979 annual average of 219.14 yen/US$ that is US$4.56M, 202% of the 1979 nominal bar of $2,255,058. The fiscal year ended March 1979 actually spans April 1978 to March 1979, so the 1978 reading was checked too: at the 1978 average of 210.44 yen/US$ the same 1 billion yen is US$4.75M against a 1978 bar of $2,025,203, or 235% of it. Above the bar on either reading. Robust to the rate: the yen would have to be weaker than about 443 per US$ for the figure to fall below the 1979 bar, and it traded roughly 194-251 through 1979. Lower end: the frame's founding-year rule. Nidec was incorporated on 23 July 1973 with 20 million yen of capital and four people, and cannot have earned before it existed. Span 1973-1979 is six years, inside the ten-year limit. NOT NARROWED: three attempts (Japanese searches for early-period 売上高 by year, Nidec's IR history pages, and the Diamond Online growth retrospective, which paywalls its revenue chart) found no revenue figure for any year between 1973 and 1978, so the crossing cannot be pinned. The yen bar in those years is about 524M yen (1976), 505M yen (1977) and 426M yen (1978), i.e. roughly half the FY1979 figure, so the true crossing is probably at the 1977-1978 end of the window and the midpoint the clocks will use, 1976, is likely one or two years early. a2: 1967 graduation from the Institute of Vocational Training (職業訓練大学校, now Polytechnic University), electrical engineering, per the Nikkei forum profile; ja.wikipedia adds that the graduation was in March 1967 and top of his class. a3: BOUNDED. ja.wikipedia states he joined the audio-equipment maker Teac after graduating and later became a director of Yamashina Seiki, but no source found gives the year he joined Teac; the March 1967 graduation brackets it from below and the July 1973 founding of Nidec from above. Japanese new-graduate hiring convention makes April 1967 very likely, but that is an inference, so the span is recorded instead. a4: Nidec is also the hit entity; no earlier venture is recorded, and ja.wikipedia notes he funded the founding by selling his Teac shareholding. a6: November 1988 listing on the Osaka Securities Exchange second section and the Kyoto Stock Exchange, fifteen years after founding; Nidec's history gives 25.8 billion yen of revenue for the fiscal year ended March 1988.

name: Morris Chang

name: An Wang
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED, WITH THE CAVEAT THE BRIEF FLAGS. The Gale biographical entry states he was estimated to be the fifth richest man in America by Forbes magazine in 1984, which is the Forbes 400 of September 1984; UPI's contemporaneous wire report on that list (upi.com/Archives/1984/09/17/The-Forbes-400-richest-Americans-Oil-electronics-and-rock-n-roll/2727464241600/, 403 to a direct fetch but indexed and quoted) names him among the 21 immigrants on it at $1.6B. CAVEAT: Forbes did not publish a self-made SCORE until the 2010s, so the roster's '(self-made score 6-10)' qualifier cannot be verified for a 1984 edition. In substance the qualifier is safe - he arrived in the US in 1945 with no capital and started the company with $600 - but no score exists to cite. PINNED rev10, not bounded, and both sides come from the same source. The International Directory of Company Histories entry for Wang Laboratories gives 'The first truly successful year for the Linasec machine was 1963, when the company recorded $300,000 in sales' and, of the following year, 'allowing Wang in fiscal 1964 to exceed $1 million in sales for the first time'. THE CONSTANT-DOLLAR CHECK IS WHAT MAKES THIS ROW WORK AND ALSO WHERE IT IS THINNEST. The 1963 nominal bar is $950,479 and $300,000 is 32% of it - clearly below. The 1964 nominal bar is $962,903 and the source says sales exceeded $1,000,000 - above, but by only about 4%. en.wikipedia's An Wang article independently gives '1964: sales reached $1,000,000', the same figure. So the crossing is dated 1964 rather than the $10M-nominal year, which Wang Laboratories did not see until 1970 ('In 1970, the huge success of calculators helped the company record its first year of $25 million in sales') - a nominal reading would have put this row six years late. BLUNT ABOUT THE MARGIN: a 4% overstatement in a round '$1 million' - i.e. a true figure anywhere below $962,903 - would move the anchor to 1965, so confidence is medium, not high. The direction of the fiscal-year ambiguity was checked and does not matter: Wang's fiscal 1964 spans mid-1963 to mid-1964, and $1M clears the 1963 bar of $950,479 as well as the 1964 bar, while the $300,000 figure is below both. NO EARLIER CROSSING: the same entry describes the company in the last two years of the 1950s as about 20 employees producing 60 to 80 units a year at about $700 each, roughly $50,000 of annual sales against a bar near $900,000, so nothing before 1963 comes close. IPO FALLBACK NOT USED AND BARRED ANYWAY: the 1967 NYSE offering of 210,000 shares is three years after the crossing. a2: Harvard PhD in applied physics, 1948, after the MS in 1946; he enrolled in September 1945. a3: JUDGMENT CALL - 1941, when he volunteered with eight classmates to design and build transmitters and radios for Nationalist troops and worked at the Central Radio Works in Kweilin (Guilin), aged 21. That is electronics hardware engineering, the same broad domain as the eventual venture, and it is his first paid technical work after the 1940 Chiao Tung degree and a year as a teaching assistant. The competing reading is 1948, when he joined Howard Aiken's Harvard Computation Laboratory and invented the magnetic core memory write-after-read cycle, which is the first COMPUTING job specifically; that reading would shorten the a3-to-a5 clock by seven years. Confidence medium for that reason, and note that a2 (1948) therefore falls after a3 (1941), which is factually correct - the wartime work preceded the American degrees. a4: June 1951, Wang Laboratories, founded as a sole proprietorship with $600 after Harvard cut back its computer research; incorporated 1955. No earlier venture is recorded. a6: the 1967 New York Stock Exchange offering.

name: Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED on Hurun's own site: the Hurun India Rich List 2014 page at hurun.net (https://www.hurun.net/en-us/info/detail?num=9E4ADEB6CB3D) ranks her 100th at INR 6,500 crore and calls her 'the only self made woman in the list'. This is a ranking, not a feature article, so the roster's citation holds. EXCLUDED, crossing_undatable, and the reason is the LOWER end of the bracket, not the upper. Upper end is available: Biocon's revenue is repeatedly reported as Rs 70 crore in 1998 (blog.shoonya.com/biocon-company/ and mynation.com, both tracing the same 'Rs 70 crore in 1998 to Rs 500 crore at the 2004 IPO' claim). At the 1998 average of about 41.3 INR/US$ that is US$16.9M, 335% of the 1998 nominal bar of $5,063,008 - above the bar even if the figure is halved. Lower end is what fails. The frame's founding-year rule gives 1978 (incorporated 29 November 1978, per Biocon's own legacy page), and 1978-1998 is a twenty-year span, double the ten-year limit. Nothing narrows it: SIX attempts (Biocon's current legacy page and the archived archive.biocon.com history page, the 2004 annual report, which prints only FY2001-FY2004; the 2004 IPO prospectus at archive.biocon.com/docs/IPO.pdf, which is a scanned image with no extractable text; the MIT Sloan 'Biocon India Group' case, which gives only US$75M of revenue around 2002; the WIPO IP Advantage case study, whose earliest figure is 2010; and repeated English-language searches for 1980s and early-1990s turnover) produced NO revenue figure for any year between 1978 and 1997. IPO FALLBACK BARRED: the July 2004 listing is at least six years after the crossing, and the qualitative record - profitable by the time Auchincloss sold to Unilever in 1989 (britannica.com/money/Kiran-Mazumdar-Shaw), India's leading enzyme producer by the mid-1990s, a three-fold plant expansion in 1996 - establishes an earlier crossing under the frame's 'what known means' rule. So the row is excluded rather than dated by the IPO. An enzyme exporter running a 20-acre Hosur Road plant from 1983 plausibly crossed in the late 1980s, but plausibly is not sourced, and dating it would be exactly the defect this project exists to prevent. a1: born 23 March 1953 in Bangalore. a2: 1975, Master Brewer, Ballarat College / University of Melbourne, after the 1973 BSc in zoology from Bangalore University; conf medium because the 1975 degree and the 1975 first job are given the same year by en.wikipedia and other coverage puts the Carlton training in 1974. a3: 1975, trainee brewer at Carlton and United Breweries, Melbourne - fermentation science, the same domain as Biocon's brewing enzymes, and her first paid technical work; the competing reading is 1978 (Biocon itself) if 'domain' is read as biotech rather than fermentation, which would collapse a3 into a4. a4: 29 November 1978, Biocon India Pvt Ltd, seed capital Rs 10,000, a JV in which Indian foreign-ownership rules left her holding 70%; it is also the hit entity, and no earlier venture is recorded. a6: the 2004 IPO, which closed at a market value of US$1.1 billion on day one.

name: Thomas Struengmann
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED: his Forbes billionaire profile (https://www.forbes.com/profile/thomas-struengmann/) gives a world rank - #314 real-time as read on 13 Aug 2026 - with $11.1B and Source of Wealth 'Pharmaceuticals, Self Made', Germany. That is the ranking itself, not a feature article, so the roster's citation holds. The roster cites the list without a self-made score, so no score needs verifying. BOUNDED rev10, both ends sourced, and the fallback never arises because no IPO exists - Hexal stayed private until the 2005 Novartis sale. Upper end: the International Directory of Company Histories entry for Hexal AG, 'By 1988, the company's revenues had topped the equivalent of EUR 28 million.' The source states the euro equivalent of a D-mark figure at the fixed 1.95583 DM/EUR conversion, i.e. DM 54.8M; at the 1988 annual average of 1.7562 DM/US$ that is US$31.2M, 849% of the 1988 nominal bar of $3,674,564. The margin is enormous and rate-insensitive: the D-mark would have to trade above 14.9 per US$ for DM 54.8M to fall below the bar, against an actual 1988 range near 1.66-1.88. Lower end: the frame's founding-year rule. Hexal Chemie GmbH & Co. KG was established in 1986 in Tegernsee, Bavaria, with five drug preparations and 22 employees, and cannot have earned before it existed. Span 1986-1988 is two years, the tightest bound in this bucket. NOT NARROWED, but the direction is knowable: the same source gives first-month sales equivalent to EUR 220,000 (DM 430,283, US$198,150 at the 1986 average of 2.1715 DM/US$). Twelve months at that rate would be US$2.38M against a 1986 bar of $3,404,329, and 1986 was a partial year in any case, so the crossing is very probably 1987 - which is also the midpoint the clocks will use. That reasoning is not sourced arithmetic about an actual 1986 total, so it does not move the bound; two further attempts (German searches for Hexal Umsatz 1987/1989 and the de.wikipedia Hexal AG article, which carries no revenue figures at all) found no annual figure between 1986 and 1988. The constant-dollar bar in D-marks for reference: DM 7.39M in 1986, DM 6.34M in 1987, DM 6.45M in 1988 - low enough that a fast-growing generics launch clears it quickly, which is why the window is short. JUDGMENT CALL on the hit entity: Hexal, not Durachemie. Durachemie was their father Ernst Struengmann's Frankfurt pharmaceutical company, which Thomas ran as CEO from 1979 and the family sold to Cyanamid in 1986 - an inherited going concern, not his own venture, so its revenue cannot fire the criterion however large it was. Sources also mention that in 1985 the family spun off one of Durachemie's subsidiaries; if that spun-off entity were treated as Hexal's start, the lower bound would move to 1985 and the span to three years, still inside the limit and still bracketing 1987, so nothing in the row turns on it. a1: born 16 February 1950 in Muelheim an der Ruhr, twin of Andreas. a2: 1977, University of Augsburg - the two company-history renderings disagree on whether the 1977 degree was an MBA (fundinguniverse) or a doctorate (encyclopedia.com), and de.wikipedia records a later Dr. rer. pol. on physician prescribing behaviour, but every version agrees on Augsburg in 1977, so the year is high confidence and the degree type is not. a3: BOUNDED 1977-1978, product manager at Schering-Plough. The source brackets it from both sides in one sentence - the 1977 degree, then the job 'initially in Lucerne before transferring to New Jersey in 1978' - so the job began in 1977 or 1978 and no source gives the month. de.wikipedia adds that he distributed pharmaceuticals for his father's firm while still a student, which would be earlier, but it is undated and therefore unusable. a4: 1986, Hexal; the 1979 Durachemie CEO role was a family appointment, not a founding, on the same convention the completed rows use for p03 and p18. a6: the sale of Hexal AG to Novartis, announced February 2005 and completed 7 June 2005, with Hexal folded into Sandoz; Forbes puts the price at about $7 billion, far above the acq50 bar, but rev10 fires roughly eighteen years earlier.

name: Zhong Huijuan
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED on the MAIN Hurun China list, not only the women's variant. The 2025 Hurun Rich List (2025胡润百富榜) places Zhong Huijuan and her daughter Sun Yuan 26th at RMB 130 billion, and the 2024 list placed her 42nd at RMB 77 billion, reported by Sina Finance (https://finance.sina.com.cn/roll/2025-10-30/doc-infvsqmh9263351.shtml and https://finance.sina.com.cn/stock/stockzmt/2024-10-29/doc-incufqpv7623934.shtml). Hurun's own site corroborates on the companion ranking: the 2025 Hurun Richest Women in China page (https://www.hurun.net/zh-cn/info/detail?num=PKHVF5M1TTQX) makes her China's richest woman at RMB 141 billion. Rankings, not feature articles, so the roster's citation holds. EXCLUDED, crossing_undatable, and the gap is the UPPER end. Lower end exists and is unusually good for a private Chinese company: Jiemian's company history states that Hansoh's first flagship product, the cephalexin sustained-release tablet Meifeng, launched in April 1997 and 当年实现收入3000万元 - RMB 30M of revenue that year (https://www.jiemian.com/article/3225325.html; drugtimes.cn/2020/07/28/479aedea22/ gives the same figure). At the 1997 annual average of 8.2898 RMB/US$ that is US$3.62M, 73% of the 1997 nominal bar of $4,985,355 - below the bar, but only by about a quarter, and the figure is the PRODUCT's sales, so company revenue was at least that and could have been over the bar. Even taken at face value it only fixes the lower end. The upper end is the problem. The earliest company-level revenue figure found anywhere is 2011, when Jiemian reports Hansoh's revenue at over RMB 3.5 billion, 78 times the 2011 bar of RMB 45.1M. 1997-2011 is a fourteen-year span and 1995-2011 is sixteen; both exceed the ten-year limit, so no legal bound exists. SEVEN attempts at a figure for 1998-2010: Hansoh's own 发展历程 and 公司简介 pages (milestones only, no revenue); the drugtimes 25-year retrospective (a 2015-2019 chart with no numbers in the text); the Jiangsu CPPCC Lianyungang pharma base paper (gives Hengrui's 2006 revenue of about RMB 1.5bn but nothing for Hansoh); the medvalley history of the Lianyungang cluster (industry aggregates only); Hengrui's 2007 annual report from cninfo, downloaded and searched - it names Jiangsu Hansoh as a related party and discloses RMB 4.23M of material purchases but no Hansoh financials; Chinese searches for the first (2006) China pharmaceutical industry top-100 list, where Hansoh ranked 69th, which never publish its revenue line; and product-level searches for Oulanning (olanzapine) and Zefei (gemcitabine), which return sample-hospital market totals for the whole molecule rather than Hansoh's sales. IPO FALLBACK BARRED: the 14 June 2019 Hong Kong listing is at least eight years after the crossing - Hansoh was already a RMB 3.5bn business in 2011 and entered China's national pharmaceutical top 100 in 2003 - so dating the row by the IPO would be wrong by well over a decade. FOR THE RECORD the bar in yuan is small: RMB 41.3M in 1997, RMB 47.3M in 2003, RMB 49.7M in 2005. A company whose single flagship product did RMB 30M in 1997 and which was a national top-100 pharmaceutical maker by 2003 almost certainly crossed between 1998 and 2001, but no source states it, and guessing inside that window is exactly what this project forbids. a1: born April 1961. a2: July 1982, BSc chemistry, Jiangsu Normal University (a later Nanjing University master's is undated and unused). a3: 1995 and equal to a4, on the p01 convention for career switchers - she taught chemistry at Lianyungang Yan'an Middle School from 1982 and had no pharmaceutical job before the venture; conf medium because some Chinese coverage instead says she resigned from a post at the Lianyungang drug administration rather than from teaching, and no source dates that post. a4: 1995, when the company was set up in Lianyungang (Hansoh's own history page dates the founding of 连云港豪森制药有限公司 to 1995). JUDGMENT CALL: sources agree her husband Sun Piaoyang and an outside investor put the company together in 1995 while he ran the state-owned Lianyungang Pharmaceutical Factory, and that she left teaching to run it as its founder; some accounts date her arrival to 1996 or 1997. The roster treats her as founder and so does this row, but it is the softest part of the identification. a6: the 14 June 2019 listing of Hansoh Pharmaceutical Group on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange (03692.HK).

name: Alfred Mann
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED, with the same caveat p20 carries. Forbes ranked him on the Forbes 400: #125 in 2005 (https://images.forbes.com/lists/2005/54/NG0I.html) and #262 in 2008 (https://www.forbes.com/lists/2008/54/400list08_Alfred-Mann_NG0I.html), the ranking pages themselves, not features. CAVEAT: Forbes only began publishing a self-made SCORE in 2014 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbes_400), and Mann died in February 2016, so the roster's '(self-made score 6-10)' qualifier cannot be verified against any edition he appeared on. In substance it is safe - a Portland shopkeeper's son who started his first company on an $11,200 Army contract - but no score exists to cite. SERIAL-FOUNDER JUDGMENT CALL, which is the whole content of this row. The frame dates the FIRST crossing among the person's own ventures, so each company was tested in founding order against the bar for its own years. (1) SPECTROLAB, founded 1956, and HELIOTEK, founded 1960 - his own until Textron bought both in 1960. The bar here is tiny: $844,870 in 1956, $897,674 in 1958, $919,417 in 1960. No revenue figure for either company in any year was found. The only sourced transaction value is contradictory. Joel West's PV-industry working paper, citing the contemporaneous Los Angeles Times report of 2 August 1960 ('Textron Buys Spectrolab of N. Hollywood', p. 23), says Textron paid $300,000 (http://www.joelwest.org/Papers/West2014a-WP.pdf, p. 5) - which is 7% of the 1960 acq50 nominal bar of $4,597,087 and points to revenue below the $919,417 rev10 bar. The International Directory of Company Histories entry for MannKind instead says Textron acquired Spectrolab and Heliotek 'for $11 million', which would be well above the acq50 bar and would imply a rev10 crossing around 1958-1960. I cannot resolve the conflict: the $300,000 figure has the contemporaneous newspaper behind it and fits a company that started on an $11,200 contract four years earlier, while the $11 million figure sits one paragraph away from that same $11,200 in the IDCH text and may be a corruption of it. Under either reading no revenue year can be pinned or bounded from above, so Spectrolab cannot carry the anchor; and after August 1960 it and Heliotek were Textron divisions that Mann ran as an employee until 1972, so their later growth is not 'the person's own venture'. (2) PACESETTER SYSTEMS is where the crossing almost certainly happened. Mann's own bio in MiniMed's FY1996 10-K states he founded it and was chairman and CEO from 1972 until 1985 (the IDCH says he started it as a research venture in 1969 and went full-time in 1972 - the two are consistent, but they give different lower bounds). It certainly crossed: by 1984 it was one of the handful of firms sharing a US pacemaker market of about $950 million and raiding Medtronic's salesforce (Circulation, 'Cardiac Pacing, 1960-1985'), and Siemens bought it in 1985 for a reported $150 million against a 1985 rev10 bar of $3,342,207. But FOUR attempts (searches for Pacesetter annual sales in 1978-1984, for the Siemens deal terms in English and German, the implantable-device.com corporate history, and Mann's SEC-filed bios) produced NO revenue figure for any year of his ownership. Bracketing from the founding to the sale gives 1972-1985, thirteen years - over the ten-year limit, and 1969-1985 is worse. So the first crossing can be neither pinned nor bounded, and the row is EXCLUDED as crossing_undatable rather than dated by the 1985 acquisition. IPO/ACQ50 FALLBACK BARRED explicitly: the frame allows it only when no earlier crossing is known, and Pacesetter's 1985 sale is a decade or more after a crossing that the market-share record makes certain. (3) MINIMED, for completeness, and this is the frustrating part: it IS datable. Its FY1996 10-K selected financial data gives net sales of $24,079,000 for 1992, 5.5 times the 1992 bar of $4,357,914, and the business dates to a 1983 first insulin pump (the IDCH says the venture began in 1979), which would make a legal 1983-1992 bound of nine years. It is not usable, because MiniMed is his THIRD or FOURTH venture and Pacesetter crossed years earlier; recording MiniMed's crossing would date the career late by roughly a decade, which is the exact defect the frame's first-crossing rule exists to prevent. a1: born 6 November 1925 in Portland, Oregon. a2: 1951 - the IDCH MannKind entry says he completed undergraduate and graduate physics at UCLA 'in 1951'; the National Academy of Engineering memorial instead says both degrees came in 1949, hence medium confidence. a3: BOUNDED 1951-1956, Technicolor, where he worked on light filters and display systems for military applications - electro-optics, the same domain as Spectrolab. Both ends are from the same source: he took the job after completing his studies (1951) and left to found Spectrolab (1956); no source dates the start month or year. a4: 1956, Spectrolab, per Mann's own bio in MiniMed's 10-K, which also confirms Heliotek in 1960 and the 1960 Textron sale of both. a6: 1985, the sale of Pacesetter Systems to Siemens (same 10-K bio; the IDCH puts the price at $150 million with about half going to Mann). MiniMed's July 1995 IPO is the alternative scale event and the first public listing of anything he founded.

name: Karsanbhai Patel
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED: multiple sources report Karsanbhai Patel on the Hurun Rich List with a stated net worth (Hurun's 2024 figure of US$9 billion, reported via goodreturns.in and iconicbillionaires.com, both naming Hurun as the source) -- a wealth-list citation with a figure attached, not a feature article. Well over a dozen distinct search/fetch attempts were made (Wikipedia pages for both novels, Britannica -- 403 blocked, CliffsNotes, SparkNotes, WordsRated's dedicated Toni-Morrison sales-statistics page, Penguin Random House's Beloved page -- 404, PBS's timeline, and multiple targeted DuckDuckGo queries combining each title with 'million copies,' 'copies in print,' and 'millions of copies'). The actual findings argue AGAINST either book having documented 1M+ sales at any point, let alone a datable year: WordsRated states Song of Solomon 'has sold 570,000 copies as of 2019' -- a specific, sourced figure that is itself only 57% of the 1M threshold, forty-two years after publication and after the book's October 1996 selection for Oprah's Book Club (confirmed via Wikipedia's Oprah's Book Club article), which is normally a major sales driver. No comparable figure -- and no 'million copies' or 'millions of copies' claim of any kind -- was found for Beloved despite specifically targeted searches; the only 'millions' language found (a New Jersey state-agency Facebook post) aggregates 'Beloved and The Bluest Eye' together with no year and no breakdown, which is exactly the kind of imprecise claim the frame's sourcing discipline says not to stretch into a dated anchor. RULING: since neither candidate can be shown to have crossed 1M, let alone dated or bounded within 10 years, a5 is unknown and the row is excluded as crossing_undatable, per the frame's explicit instruction that print sales for this era are reported inconsistently and an honest exclusion is an acceptable outcome. hit_entity names both candidates considered rather than asserting a winner, since neither was confirmed. a6: 1993 Nobel Prize in Literature retained as a later, definite, well-sourced recognition event despite a5's exclusion, matching the p27 Kim Sung-joo convention of populating a6 with a real dated event independent of the excluded a5.

name: Youssou N'Dour
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED: N'Dour won the Grammy for Best Contemporary World Music Album (Egypt) in 2005, per Wikipedia -- an official Recording Academy award, not a feature article. a1: born 1 Oct 1959, Dakar (Wikipedia). a2: unknown -- multiple sources agree he dropped out of school to pursue music full-time; no source gives a final schooling year, so left unknown rather than guessed rather than treating 'dropped out' itself as datable. a3: signed a paid singing contract with Ibra Kasse's Star Band at Kasse's 'Miami Club' in Dakar in 1976 at age 16 -- his first paid domain job, distinct from forming his own group (Wikipedia). a4: formed his own band, Etoile de Dakar, in 1979 -- 'first venture' under the founding convention (Wikipedia; the source also gives the later Super Etoile de Dakar rename as 1981, not used as a4 since Etoile de Dakar is the earlier founding). a5 -- THE HARD ANCHOR, RESOLVED (not excluded): the task brief flagged this as possibly unsourceable given how poorly documented African-market cassette sales are. The 2004 Egypt album (his eventual Grammy winner) is explicitly documented at only ~400,000 copies worldwide, below the 1M bar, so it does not qualify. Checking backward, N'Dour's 1994 duet with Neneh Cherry, '7 Seconds,' has a Wikipedia certifications table with per-country GOLD/PLATINUM awards: France 250,000, Germany 250,000, UK 420,000, Austria 25,000, Netherlands 50,000, Switzerland 25,000, Spain 25,000, Australia 35,000, New Zealand (Platinum) 10,000 -- summing to 1,090,000 units as a FLOOR (certification thresholds are minimums; true sales in large markets like the UK/France/Germany are typically well above the certified floor). This is before counting the countries where it charted #1 with no certification data available at all (France #1 for 16 consecutive weeks -- a chart record at the time --, Finland, Iceland, Italy, Belgium-Wallonia all #1; Netherlands #2; Eurochart Hot 100 #2). The song is credited jointly to N'Dour and Cherry but is unambiguously N'Dour's own recorded work under the same 'co-credited work still counts' logic used for jointly founded ventures elsewhere in this dataset. Dated to 1994, the release/chart-peak year, at medium confidence since the certification awards themselves may postdate 1994 slightly even though the #1 chart runs happened within 1994. MARGIN FLAG: the certified-floor sum (1,090,000) clears the 1M bar by only about 9% -- under the ~20% caution threshold -- though this is a floor, not an actual-sales figure, so the true margin is very likely much larger; flagged per instructions regardless. a6: 2005 Grammy win (Egypt) retained as the later, larger-stage recognition event.

name: Ryan Petersen
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED: Y Combinator's own blog post announcing its inaugural 'Top Companies List by Revenue' (ycombinator.com/blog/yc-top-companies-list-by-revenue, ranking YC alumni by 2022 net revenue) includes Flexport, corroborated by Flexport's own LinkedIn post celebrating the inclusion and a repeat listing in YC's 2024 update covering 2023 revenue -- a genuine third-party ranking naming a first year, not a feature article. a1: Wikipedia states 'born 1980 or 1981' with no source resolving which; multiple secondary aggregators repeat the same either/or, so recorded as a bounded 1980-1981 span rather than guessed. a2: MBA, Columbia Business School, class of 2008 (business.columbia.edu's own alumni bio page is titled 'Ryan Petersen '08,' Columbia's standard class-year notation; the page itself returned 403 on direct fetch so this is confirmed only via the URL/title rather than fetched body text, hence medium not high confidence), after a 2002 BA in Economics from UC Berkeley (Wikipedia). a3/a4: R1 CONVENTION (the p26 Roddick precedent) -- no employer-paid domain job precedes his first venture, so a3 = a4. Wikipedia states that 'at age 17, he started an import-export business with his brother David, buying goods from China and selling them on eBay' -- given the birth-year uncertainty (1980-1981) compounding with the imprecision of 'age 17' itself (which straddles two calendar years depending on birthday), this is recorded as a bounded 1997-1999 span at low confidence rather than a single guessed year. This teenage venture, not the later formally named ImportGenius, is treated as the 'first thing founded' under the convention used throughout this dataset. a5 -- REV10, IMPORTGENIUS CHECKED FIRST PER INSTRUCTIONS, RULED OUT: ImportGenius (founded 2006 per Wikipedia -- one earlier source said 2007, not used since Wikipedia and a TechCrunch retrospective both independently say 2006) was checked for an earlier rev10 crossing than Flexport, as instructed, since it is the earlier-founded venture. No dollar figure for any year was found across multiple attempts (Wikipedia's ImportGenius article gives no revenue at all; a Contrary Research report states only that it 'was still a multi-million-dollar business as of February 2022,' sixteen years after founding -- outside the 10-year bounding window even if treated as an upper bound, and 'multi-million' is too imprecise to know if it was ever above or below the ~$7.4-7.6M threshold that applied in the relevant years). A TechCrunch profile of Petersen additionally describes ImportGenius as having 'eventually plateaued,' which argues against assuming a large, industry-leading scale by any particular year -- i.e. there is no qualitative claim of the kind frame.md would accept as establishing that an earlier, merely-undated crossing occurred. ImportGenius therefore contributes no usable anchor and is ruled out, not treated as an unresolved earlier crossing that would bar dating Flexport. FLEXPORT, THE ANCHOR USED: Flexport was founded in 2013 (Wikipedia). Its Wikipedia article quotes the company telling Chinese outlet 36Kr in May 2015 that it was 'on pace to generate $60 million in sales for 2015' -- a figure roughly 8x the 2015 nominal rev10 bar of $7,362,080 (python3 -m src.cpi 2015), comfortably above threshold with no margin concern. Per frame.md's explicit rule that 'the founding year is a valid lower bound' and that 'where the earliest published figure is already above threshold, bound the crossing from the entity's founding to that figure's year,' the crossing is bounded 2013-2015 (a 3-year span, well inside the 10-year cap) rather than pinned to a single year, since no month-level revenue trajectory within that window was sourced. (A separate, lower-quality aggregator site claims Flexport revenue was '$2 million in 2014,' which would tighten the crossing to 2015 specifically and is consistent with the bound used, but was not relied on directly given the source's reliability, and the founding-year bound already satisfies the frame's sourcing rule without it.) IPO/ACQ50 FALLBACK NOT NEEDED: rev10 fires directly via the bound above. a6: 2022 Series E ($935M raised, $8B post-money valuation, per Wikipedia) retained as the later, larger-scale event.

Thus 2016 = USD5,062,600 versus bar USD7,454,953, margin -USD2,392,353; 2017 = USD18,026,850 versus bar USD7,613,770, margin +USD10,413,080 (2.368x). The crossing is therefore 2017, Canva, rev10 primary; the 2015 figure was undisclosed (https://www.smartcompany.com.au/finance/canva-raises-7-7-million-prepares-to-launch-canva-for-work/), while the available ASIC-derived series identifies 2016 below and 2017 above. name: Rana el Kaliouby

FUNDRAISING: Affectiva announced a USD 26 million round on 11 April 2019, bringing total invested capital to USD 53 million (https://www.affectiva.com/news-item/affectiva-raises-26-million-to-fast-track-human-perception-ai-in-automotive-and-conversational-interfaces/); funding is not revenue and does not fire or bar rev10. a1: born in Cairo in 1978 per the University of Wisconsin biography (https://interfaces.che.wisc.edu/rana-el-kaliouby/), corroborated only to age 39 by Fortune in 2018; no reliable exact day or month was found, so confidence is medium. a2: University of Cambridge's record states that her PhD dissertation was submitted in March 2005 for the Cambridge doctorate (https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/techreports/UCAM-CL-TR-636.html); this is the final dated degree. a3: UNKNOWN after multiple attempts. AUC quotes her saying her first job ever was assistant analyst in Academic Computing Services but gives no year (https://www.aucegypt.edu/news/students-pyramid; https://www.aucegypt.edu/news/stories/alumna-rana-el-kaliouby-aucs-newest-youngest-trustee). Her public professional chronology dates a later Cambridge Research Associate role to 2001-2005 and MIT documents her as a postdoctoral associate in 2006 (https://news.mit.edu/2006/media-sensors), but neither can replace the known earlier, undated AUC job. No unsupported date or range is inferred. a4: 2009 Affectiva founding, high confidence. a5: 2021 Smart Eye acquisition under acq50 fallback, high confidence. a6: UNKNOWN after two attempts. The 2021 acquisition is already a5; afterward Affectiva ceased being an independent venture and el Kaliouby's Smart Eye role concerns the acquirer, not a later scale event for her own venture. notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED: the Computer History Museum profile labels Federico Faggin a 2009 Fellow for his work on the Intel 4004, and the Museum's 2009 Fellow Awards page names him among the honorees and dates the event to 20 October 2009 (https://computerhistory.org/profile/federico-faggin/; https://computerhistory.org/events/2009-fellow-awards/). The $100M scale is independently corroborated by the International Directory-derived company history, which says Zilog generated $50M annually within a few years and later peaked above $100M before the 1981-1982 downturn (https://www.referenceforbusiness.com/history/Vi-Z/ZiLOG-Inc.html). NOT PINNED EARLIER after multiple attempts: the editorial summary's 1977 sales under $5M straddle the 1977 bar of $1,882,321, so they do not establish above or below; a synthesized secondary claim of $1M in 1976 was rejected because no traceable original citation was found, though its audit bar was computed at $1,767,394; the company-history claim of $50M within a few years has no revenue year and therefore cannot supply an exact endpoint; targeted searches for exact 1976-1980 total sales found no annual filing or contemporary figure. A 1983 Dataquest profile explicitly states estimated 1982 European revenue of $22M, 7.340x the 1982 bar of $2,997,425, but this is later and does not narrow the selected upper bound (http://archive.computerhistory.org/resources/access/text/2013/04/102723447-05-01-acc.pdf). Secondary pages sometimes say 1980, so the primary filings' 1981 date is used; the original 51% step's date/price and the full acquisition price remain unstated and are not inferred. For 1959 to have been above the bar the 1954 base would have to be wrong by a factor of 3.5, so the crossing is not before 1960. So the crossing is at or before 1969. Nine-year span, inside the frame's ten-year limit. The crossing year itself is genuinely unpinned: the chronology gives growth rates (1955 +21.5%, 1964 +26%, 1970 +50%) but no absolute figure between 1959 and 1974, when Adolf Wuerth KG first passed DM 100 million (group DM 217 million) -- and 1974 is too far from 1959 to serve as the upper end. There is no IPO or acquisition to fall back on: Wuerth has never been listed, so the fallback question does not arise. SERIAL FOUNDER CHECK: no earlier venture, and none is possible -- he was taken out of the Oberrealschule at 14 and put straight into his father's firm, where he spent his whole working life; Adolf Wuerth KG is his only business. a2: 1949, the year his father 'meldete ihn von der Oberrealschule ab' (de.wikipedia). name: Konrad Zuse
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED: computerhistory.org/profile/konrad-zuse/ names him a 1999 Computer History Museum Fellow (roster URL re-confirmed), citation "For his invention of the first program-controlled, electromechanical, digital computer and the first high-level programming language, 'Plankalkuel'". a1: born 22 June 1910 (Neue Deutsche Biographie via deutsche-biographie.de; de.wikipedia agrees). a2: Diplom in Bauingenieurwesen, TH Berlin-Charlottenburg, July 1935 -- the last and only credential completed (Abitur 1928). a3: July 1935, structural engineer at Henschel Flugzeug-Werke, Berlin-Schoenefeld, his first paid engineering post and the calculation drudgery that produced the machines; his first paid work on computing hardware specifically was the Henschel S1 special-purpose computer from about 1940, also as a Henschel employee, hence conf medium on the choice of 1935. SERIAL FOUNDER CHECK -- MATERIAL: Zuse KG (1949) is NOT his first venture. He set up "Dipl.-Ing. K. Zuse Ingenieurbuero und Apparatebau" in Berlin (NDB dates the name to May 1936, formally constituted April 1941; de.wikipedia gives 1941), and after the war a short-lived "Zuse-Ingenieurbuero, Hopferau" with Harro Stucken in autumn 1946. Neither can have been the crossing: the Berlin firm never exceeded about 20 staff, worked on individual development contracts (Henschel S1/S2, the Z4) rather than a product line, published no revenue, and was destroyed in 1945; the 1941 nominal rev10 bar was $456,603, about 1.14M Reichsmark at the official 2.50 RM/USD parity, which a 20-person Berlin workshop is not documented anywhere as approaching, and the Hopferau office was a two-man consultancy. No source documents a crossing by either, so the hit entity is Zuse KG, founded 1 August 1949 in Neukirchen (Kreis Huenfeld) with five to eight employees. a4 is recorded as 1941 (the formally constituted Berlin firm) rather than 1949, since the earlier venture is what a4 asks for; 1936 is the alternative reading and is why conf is medium. a5 rev10 = BOUNDED 1954-1961, a 7-year span, both ends sourced, against the constant-2026-dollar bar for each year, NOT $10M nominal. CURRENCY: DM/USD from the de.wikipedia Deutsche Mark rate table -- the Bretton Woods parity 4.20 DM/USD held from 1949 (table entry "1950/52: 4,2") to the March 1961 revaluation, and the table gives 4,0221 DM/USD for 1961. LOWER END, below the bar: the Neue Deutsche Biographie states of the early Zuse KG that Konrad Zuse "der Umsatz 1954 bis auf 1,3 Mio. DM anwachsen liess" -- 1954 turnover DM 1,300,000. The 1954 nominal rev10 bar is $835,552 (python -m src.cpi 1954), which at 4.20 DM/USD is DM 3,509,318, so 1954 revenue was 37% of the bar, clearly below. UPPER END, above the bar: the same NDB entry records that by 1961 turnover had reached about DM 9 million with more than 300 employees. The 1961 nominal bar is $928,736, or DM 3,735,466 at 4,0221 DM/USD, so DM 9,000,000 is 241% of the bar -- above by a wide margin, and above even on the pre-revaluation 4.20 rate (231%). The crossing therefore happened between 1954 and 1961; the intervening years are exactly the Z11 (from 1955, series production) and Z22 (from 1958, 55 units at about DM 250,000 each) ramp, and no source pins the single year. Neither end is a qualitative claim: both are DM figures from the NDB. FALLBACK NOT AVAILABLE AND NOT NEEDED: Zuse KG never listed; control passed to Rheinstahl/Brown Boveri in 1964 and to Siemens in 1967, both after the crossing, and no purchase price is published for either. a6: 1964, when Brown, Boveri & Cie took complete control after Zuse KG's financial difficulties, the company then standing at 1,200 employees and an order book above DM 25 million -- the later, larger-scale event, following this dataset's convention of a listing or change-of-control as the scale marker.

name: Gautam Adani

Lower end: Adani Exports was founded in 1988 as a partnership firm with a capital of Rs 5 lakh (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adani_Group; Forbes; adani.com timeline, 'Mr. Gautam Adani established Adani Exports that deals in agricultural commodities and power in Ahmedabad, Gujarat'), roughly $35-40k at the era's ~13 INR/USD -- about 1% of the 1988 constant-dollar rev10 bar of $3,674,564 -- and a company cannot earn before it exists. Under frame.md a dated qualitative industry-leading claim establishes that the crossing had already occurred; India's single largest net foreign-exchange earner in 1998 was necessarily orders of magnitude above that year's bar of $5,063,008 (about Rs 21 crore at the period's ~41 INR/USD). FLAGGED: the upper end of this bracket is a QUALITATIVE SCALE CLAIM doing the dating work, and its primary wording is the company's own -- acceptable for rev10 bounding (frame.md's 'company's own claim is not a ranking' rule governs rank1, not revenue), and independently repeated by Wikipedia, but it is the weakest link on this row. Neither version supplies a dated completed credential, so unknown is recorded rather than a guess, following p34 and p73. a3: 1978, diamond sorter for Mahendra Brothers in Mumbai -- his first paid work in the commodity trade that the hit entity is built on. a6: 2007, the Mundra Port and Special Economic Zone IPO, '116 times oversubscription' per Adani's own timeline.

name: Mariya Nurislamova

Her completed credential is a BBA from Baruch College (Zicklin School of Business), CUNY; forumdaily states she finished it in two years and that her earlier Perm Polytechnic applied-mathematics course was LEFT INCOMPLETE (Equilar's listing of two Perm "B.S." degrees is contradicted by her own account, so it is not used). Confidence medium: the dates come from a LinkedIn-derived aggregator, corroborated in company list but not in dates by nocap.blog. a6: 2019, when she stated an annual turnover of $60M and "more than $5 million per month" to forumdaily -- a later, larger-scale event than the a5 crossing. name: Jim Ratcliffe
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED: Sunday Times Rich List 2025, rank 7 -- "Sir Jim Ratcliffe | 17.046 | Industry (Ineos)" -- fetched from en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunday_Times_Rich_List_2025, which reproduces the ranked table naming him; corroborated by his own Wikipedia article, which records the Sunday Times Rich List 2018 naming him Britain's wealthiest individual at GBP 21.05bn. The roster's note that thetimes.com returns a 1.3KB shell naming nobody was not re-tested; the Wikipedia reproduction of the ranked table names the person and the rank, which is the standard the brief asks for. SERIAL-FOUNDER CALL -- THE HIT ENTITY IS INSPEC, NOT INEOS. THIS IS THE MAIN JUDGMENT ON THIS ROW AND IT MOVES THE ANCHOR SIX YEARS EARLIER. The roster frames Ineos (1998) as the venture and Ratcliffe's earlier years as "a long apprenticeship as an employee engineer and then a private-equity operator". That framing does not survive checking. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ineos states in its own history section that Ineos "traces its roots to Inspec, established in 1992 by Jim Ratcliffe and John Hollowood"; businesschief.eu and business-sale.com both use co-founding language for the same event (Ratcliffe, then a director at Advent International, partnered with Dr John Hollowood to buy a chemicals division out of BP for about $50M in a management buy-IN, with Hollowood as chairman and Ratcliffe as chief executive). Inspec Group plc was a newly formed company that acquired assets -- structurally the identical move to Ineos in 1998, which was also a new company formed to buy an existing plant (the Antwerp site, for GBP 84M). Bought is not inherited, so frame.md's going-concern bar does not fire: he did not take over a family firm, he formed the acquiring vehicle. Under the study's rule that the hit is the FIRST venture to cross, Inspec displaces Ineos. The counter-case is recorded honestly: at the moment of the 1992 deal he was on Advent's payroll and Advent backed it, so it can be read as a PE portfolio-company CEO appointment rather than his own venture. Two independent sources use founding language and none describes him as merely hired, so the founding reading is taken. Nothing earlier qualifies -- BP, the unnamed pharmaceutical company, Esso, Courtaulds and Advent are all employers, not ventures -- so 1992 Inspec is also a4. BOUNDED rev10 1992-1994, both ends sourced, QUALITATIVE SCALE CLAIM DOING THE DATING WORK (flagged as the brief requires). LOWER END: the founding-year rule -- Inspec did not exist before the 1992 buy-in and cannot have earned before it existed. UPPER END: businesschief.eu records that "1994: Inspec floated on London Stock Exchange valued at $125 million". The 1994 rev10 bar is $4,603,299 nominal; a specialty-chemicals manufacturer carrying a $125M public-market valuation is 27x the bar in valuation terms and cannot plausibly be under $4.6M of sales, and the business it was built on was itself bought from BP for about $50M in 1992 -- 11x the 1992 bar of $4,357,914 in purchase price alone. frame.md explicitly permits a qualitative scale claim to establish that a crossing occurred, leaving only the year to be bounded, and that is exactly what is happening here: NO STATED REVENUE FIGURE FOR INSPEC IN ANY YEAR WAS FOUND despite targeted searching (Laporte plc's Wikipedia page gives only the ~$1bn 1998 takeover price; the only Inspec-specific earnings number found anywhere is that the acquisition contributed GBP 18.1M to Laporte's 1998 pre-tax profits in a four-month stub period, itself far above that year's GBP-converted bar but too late to narrow this bound). The true crossing is most likely 1992 itself, since the entity began life owning an operating BP division rather than as a startup with no sales, so the midpoint of 1993 is if anything late. Span is two years. NO CURRENCY CONVERSION APPLIED: both load-bearing figures ($50M purchase price, $125M flotation valuation) are already quoted in US dollars by the source, so they compare directly against the nominal USD bars. a1: born 18 October 1952, Failsworth, Lancashire (Wikipedia). a2: 1980, MBA in finance from London Business School, studied 1978-1980 and funded by his then employer Esso -- this is the last credential completed, later than his 2:1 in chemical engineering from the University of Birmingham in 1974 (both from Wikipedia, LBS corroborated by businesschief.eu). a3: 1974, medium confidence and a judgment call. On graduating from Birmingham in 1974 he joined BP as a chemical engineer -- squarely the domain that produced the hit -- but was dismissed after three days because eczema made him unsuitable for work with toxic chemicals. He then worked as a trainee accountant at a pharmaceutical company and joined Esso, and spent over a decade at Courtaulds, a chemicals and fabrics producer, into his mid-thirties. No source gives a year for the Esso or Courtaulds start, so the only datable entry into the chemical industry is the 1974 BP hiring; its three-day duration is why confidence is medium rather than high. a6: 2005, the $9bn purchase of BP's Innovene, which per en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ineos "roughly quadrupled Ineos's turnover, which was previously around $8 billion" -- a later, far larger-scale event than the a5 crossing, and the point at which the Ineos rollup became a top-tier global petrochemicals business.

name: Lakshmi Mittal
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED: Sunday Times Rich List 2025, rank 8 -- "Lakshmi Mittal and family | 15.444 | Steel" -- fetched from en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunday_Times_Rich_List_2025, which reproduces the ranked table naming him. Corroborated in depth by his own Wikipedia article, which tabulates his Rich List placings across years (1st in 2006 at GBP 14.88bn, 1st in 2008 at GBP 27.70bn, 7th in 2015 and 2024). INHERITED-FIRM CHECK, THE ONE THE ASSIGNMENT FLAGS: his father Mohanlal Mittal ran the family steel business Nippon Denro Ispat, which Lakshmi joined as a TRAINEE in 1970 after graduating. That going concern is barred as a hit entity by frame.md and is not used. His own venture is PT Ispat Indo, established 1976 in Sidoarjo, East Java, Indonesia -- described by Wikipedia as "his inaugural independent steel factory", founded when Indian government curbs on domestic steel production pushed him abroad at age 26. He built it greenfield rather than taking it over. The Indian family assets stayed with his brothers Pramod and Vinod at the 1994 split, which confirms the separation of the two lines. SERIAL-FOUNDER CHECK: no earlier venture found. Between his 1970 entry into his father's firm and the 1976 Indonesian venture he was an employee of the family business; Ispat Indo is the first thing he founded and also the first to cross. rev10 1978, QUALITATIVE SCALE CLAIM DOING THE DATING WORK -- FLAGGED AS THE BRIEF REQUIRES, AND THIS IS THE WEAKEST POINT OF THE ROW. No source gives a revenue figure for PT Ispat Indo in any year. What is sourced is (a) the plant "opened in Sidoarjo, East Java, Indonesia in 1978 and made money right away" (globalindian.com), and (b) that it "started off as a 60,000T per annum greenfield rolling facility for wire rods" before expanding to around 800,000T of melting/casting/rolling over later decades. The 1978 rev10 bar is $2,025,203 nominal. Wire rod sold for roughly $300/tonne in 1978, so nameplate 60,000 tonnes is on the order of $18M -- roughly 9x the bar -- and the plant would clear the bar at about 11% of nameplate utilisation in its opening year. A first-year crossing is therefore safe by a very wide margin even on a heavily discounted ramp, which is why this is recorded as the exact year 1978 rather than a bounded range: the entity did not exist as a producer before 1978 (so nothing earlier is possible) and it cleared the bar in its first operating year. Confidence is medium, not high, because the crossing rests on capacity plus a stated price level rather than on a published sales figure, and because the plant's 1976 establishment date differs from its 1978 opening date across sources. NO CURRENCY CONVERSION NEEDED: steel wire rod is priced and traded in US dollars and the capacity-derived figure is already in USD; no rupiah or rupee account was used. a1: born 15 June 1950, Sadulpur, Rajasthan (Wikipedia). a2: 1970, B.Com with first-class honours from St. Xavier's College, University of Calcutta (globalindian.com; Wikipedia confirms the college and degree but gives no year, so confidence is medium rather than high). a3: 1970, joined his father's Nippon Denro Ispat as a trainee immediately on graduating -- the same year as a2, and squarely in the steel domain that produced the hit. He had already been working evening shifts at the steel mill from age 19 while studying, so an argument exists for 1969, but 1970 is the first dated full-time role and is what is recorded. a4: 1976, the establishment of PT Ispat Indo, not the 1978 plant opening -- a4 is the founding of the venture, a5 the crossing. a6: 2006-07, the hostile takeover of Arcelor creating ArcelorMittal, the world's largest steel producer -- a later, vastly larger-scale event than the a5 crossing; recorded as 2006, the year the bid succeeded (Wikipedia).

name: Carver Mead
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED: computerhistory.org/profile/carver-mead/ names him as a 2002 Computer History Museum Fellow with the citation "for his contributions in pioneering the automation, methodology and teaching of integrated circuit design" -- an official award page naming the person, fetched directly. SERIAL-FOUNDER CALL, AND IT IS THE HARD PART OF THIS ROW. Wikipedia states Mead "has been involved in the founding of at least 20 companies" and lists eight of the significant ones. By founding date the candidates are Lexitron (word processing), Silicon Compilers Inc. 1981, Actel 1985, Synaptics 1986, Sonix/Sonic Innovations 1991, Silerity (sold to Viewlogic 1995), Foveon c.1999 and Impinj (2000s). LEXITRON CONSIDERED AND REJECTED AS THE HIT ENTITY, WITH THE REASON RECORDED: Lexitron dates from 1969 (the Computer History Archives video Wikipedia cites is titled "Lexitron Word Processing Computer Origin & History 1969-1984") and was acquired by Raytheon in 1977-78, so if it counted it would move this row's a4 and a5 back by more than a decade. It does not count, for two independent reasons. (1) Mead's founder role is asserted in exactly one place -- a bare bullet in Wikipedia's company list, sourced to a Vimeo video -- and three separate searches pairing "Carver Mead" with Lexitron found no other source connecting him to the company, no year for his involvement, and no description of what "involved in the founding" meant. (2) Even granting the role, Lexitron's crossing is undatable: no revenue or sales figure for Lexitron in any year surfaced in any source, and the Raytheon purchase price is not published either, so neither a rev10 date, a bound, nor an acq50 fallback can be built. Recording Lexitron would require inventing both the year and the scale. It is therefore excluded from consideration and Silicon Compilers Inc. is used, with this caveat flagged for re-checking. CONTESTED FOUNDER STATUS AT SCI, ALSO FLAGGED: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carver_Mead states that "Mead, Johannsen, Edmund K. Cheng and others formed Silicon Compilers Inc. (SCI) in 1981", citing David Lammers in IEEE Spectrum and the Computer History Museum's oral history of Edmund Cheng. semiengineering.com's entity page instead lists SCI's founders as David Johannsen, Edmund K. Cheng, L. John Doerr III and Peter Rip, omitting Mead. Wikipedia's version rests on two named primary-ish sources including a CHM oral history and is preferred, but the conflict is real and is recorded rather than smoothed over. SCI grew directly out of Mead's own Caltech work: he and his PhD student David L. Johannsen built the first silicon compiler (Johannsen's "Bristle Blocks", 1979). BOUNDED rev10 1981-1989, both ends sourced, span 8 years, midpoint 1985. LOWER END: the founding-year rule -- SCI was formed in 1981 and cannot have earned before it existed. UPPER END: techmonitor.ai reports that Silicon Compiler Systems "was doing $45m in 1989" with an installed base of over 1,700 chip design seats and close to 400 employees, when Mentor Graphics agreed to buy it for about $110M in 6.3M new shares. The 1989 rev10 bar is $3,851,613 nominal, so $45M is 11.7x the bar -- no margin problem at all. CAVEAT ON THE UPPER END: Silicon Compiler Systems was created in 1987 from the merger of Silicon Design Labs with Silicon Compilers Inc. (same source), so the $45M is the merged company's, not SCI's alone; even attributing only half of it to the SCI side leaves roughly $22M, still 5.8x the bar, so the conclusion is unaffected by the attribution. NOT NARROWED: targeted searching for an SCI revenue figure for 1984, 1985 or 1986 found none; the company was private and its best-known mid-1980s milestone (designing one of the key chips for DEC's MicroVAX, and the 1986 VTC process deal for Genesil users) carries no dollar figure. The 1990 Mentor acquisition at $110M would clear the acq50 bar easily, but the fallback is BARRED here because an earlier crossing is known to have occurred (the 1989 revenue figure itself proves it), exactly as frame.md requires. a1: born 1 May 1934, Bakersfield, California (Wikipedia; CHM profile confirms 1934 and Bakersfield). a2: 1960, PhD in Electrical Engineering from Caltech, after a BS in 1956 and an MS in 1957 -- 1960 is given by Wikipedia (citing Caltech's own CNS faculty page and the Caltech Archives oral history), by Caltech's own carvermead.caltech.edu/biography ("BS ('56), MS ('57) and PhD ('60)") and by lemelson.mit.edu. DISCREPANCY NOTED: the Computer History Museum's own Fellow profile says the PhD was 1959; it is outvoted 3-1 by Caltech's own pages and is not used. a3: 1960, LOW CONFIDENCE AND THE WEAKEST ANCHOR ON THIS ROW. Mead never left Caltech -- he was a teaching assistant as an undergraduate, taught through graduate school, and retired in 1999 after 40-plus years on the faculty -- and no fetchable source gives the year he converted from student/TA to faculty. Two attempts (caltech.edu's "The Life of a Caltech Lifer" feature and Caltech's own carvermead.caltech.edu biography) both describe the continuous career without dating the appointment. 1960 is recorded as the year his independent work in the hit's domain begins: it is both the PhD year and the year Wikipedia records him as "the first person to describe and demonstrate a three-terminal solid-state device based on the operating principles of electron tunneling and hot-electron transport". a4: 1981, Silicon Compilers Inc. See the Lexitron discussion above -- if Mead's Lexitron founding role were ever properly sourced with a year, a4 would move to about 1969. a6: 1990, Mentor Graphics' acquisition of Silicon Compiler Systems for about $110M -- a later, larger-scale event than the a5 crossing (techmonitor.ai).

name: Stephen Lake
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED TWICE OVER: ycombinator.com/companies/north names "Stephen Lake (Founder/CEO)" with the one-liner "Wearable computing hardware: biosignal gesture recognition" (founded 2012, batch Winter 2013, status Acquired), and North is entry 35 of the 91-company Y Combinator Top Companies list, verified by downloading https://yc-oss.github.io/api/companies/top.json with curl and indexing it rather than trusting the roster's claim. SERIAL-FOUNDER CHECK: no earlier venture. Lake, Matthew Bailey and Aaron Grant founded Thalmic Labs in 2012, the year all three took a BASc in mechatronics engineering at Waterloo; no source records any prior company or employer, and his other venture, Jetson, post-dates the 2020 acquisition. Thalmic Labs (renamed North in 2018) is both his first venture and the hit entity. acq50 FALLBACK USED -- FLAGGED, BECAUSE frame.md MAKES THE FALLBACK THE RARE EXCEPTION AND THIS ROW CLAIMS IT. a5 = 2020, Google's acquisition of North, reported by The Globe and Mail at approximately US$180M and relayed by BetaKit and silicon.co.uk; terms were never officially disclosed, so confidence is medium. The 2020 acq50 bar is $40,195,159 nominal, so $180M is 4.5x the bar -- no margin problem. NO CURRENCY CONVERSION NEEDED: BetaKit states the figure in US dollars. WHY THE FALLBACK IS NOT BARRED HERE, SET OUT IN FULL BECAUSE IT IS THE CONTESTABLE PART OF THIS ROW. frame.md bars the fallback whenever an earlier rev10 crossing is KNOWN, including on a purely qualitative claim that the venture was already large or profitable. No such claim exists for this company, and the sourced facts point the other way. What is sourced about scale is all funding and headcount, never revenue: about $200M raised in equity and debt by 2019, "one of the highest-funded pre-IPO companies in Canada" (TechCrunch, Aug 2019), 400-plus employees before roughly 150 were laid off in 2019, and ~200 at acquisition. What is sourced about commercial performance is uniformly bad: the Myo armband ($199.99, launched 1 May 2015) was discontinued in October 2018, Focals 1.0 shipped January 2019 and was discontinued that December, and Focals 2.0 never shipped at all. The only revenue-shaped numbers anywhere are from the February 2013 preorder campaign -- TechCrunch's "10,000 Pre-Orders In 2 Days, Which Adds Up To $1.5M In Sales", about $4M of preorders in the first month, and roughly 30,000 preorders reported later in 2013 -- all of which sit BELOW the 2013 rev10 bar of $7,235,970, and all of which are preorders for a device that did not ship until late 2014. Two further attempts (a WebSearch for Myo units sold and revenue for 2015-2016, and Brave-index queries for Focals unit sales) turned up no annual revenue figure for any year of this company's existence, from any source. Since no source establishes -- quantitatively or qualitatively -- that revenue ever reached the bar, the earlier crossing is not "known" and the fallback is permitted. An adversarial re-check should test exactly this: if a Myo or Focals unit-sales figure exists for any single year above roughly $7.4M, this row becomes a bounded rev10 instead. NOTE ON THE WEB SEARCH BUDGET: the session's shared 200-call WebSearch budget was exhausted partway through this person, so the last stage of research ran on WebFetch and curl against the Brave Search index only. a1: BOUNDED 1989-1990. Forbes' 30 Under 30 entry, published 18 January 2017, gives Lake's age as 27, which places his birth between January 1989 and January 1990. No source gives a birth date directly, so the bound rather than a point year is recorded. a2: 2012, BASc in mechatronics engineering, University of Waterloo -- high confidence, from the university's own engineering news page, which states that Lake, Bailey and Grant "all graduated with a BASc in Mechatronics in 2012", corroborated by uwaterloo.ca/alumni/news/interview-thalmic-labs describing them as "the three graduates of the UWaterloo Mechatronics Engineering Class of '12". This is a completed degree, not a dropout. a3: 2012, set equal to a4 under the R1 convention (the p26 Roddick / Sara Blakely precedent): the founding of Thalmic Labs is his first role in wearable-computing hardware, and no employer-paid job in the domain precedes it -- Waterloo's mechatronics programme is co-op, so he will have had student work terms, but no source names an employer or a year for any of them. Confidence low for that reason. a4: 2012, Thalmic Labs, founded in the same year the degree completed -- the near-zero education-to-venture gap the roster selected this row to test is real and confirmed. a6: unknown. The 2020 Google acquisition is already a5; nothing larger or later followed for this entity, which was absorbed and whose Focals support ended 31 July 2020.

name: Aleksandr Konotopskyi

name: Jill Lepore
